↩ ◇ Note. The completion formula. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest deliberate echoes of Gen 2:1–3: "thus the heavens and the earth were finished" — the same Hebrew root kalah ("complete") and the same liturgical cadence. The intertextual signal is precise: the construction of the tabernacle is presented as a creation-act parallel to the creation of the cosmos. The same parallel runs through the entire creation/tabernacle architecture: God creates in seven days; the tabernacle instructions come in seven divine speeches (Exod 25:1, 30:11, 30:17, 30:22, 30:34, 31:1, 31:12); creation culminates in Sabbath rest, and tabernacle instructions end with Sabbath command (31:12–17). The structural parallel encodes one of the OT’s deepest theological claims: the tabernacle is microcosm. Where Eden was the original meeting-place between God and humanity (Gen 3:8) and was lost, the tabernacle is the engineered restoration of that meeting-place at micro-scale. The verse is the formal closure of that creation-restoration narrative arc.

↩ ◇ Note. The high priest’s ephod. The ephod — a sleeveless apron-like vestment of gold thread woven with blue, purple, and scarlet — is one of the most enigmatic objects in OT cult. Its function is not just decorative: the ephod holds the breastpiece (28:15–30) with its twelve tribal stones and the Urim and Thummim (28:30, the oracular stones), making it the priestly oracular vestment proper. David twice uses an ephod for divine consultation (1 Sam 23:9, 30:7). In post-monarchic narratives, ephods proliferate problematically: Gideon makes an unauthorized ephod that becomes a snare (Judg 8:27), Micah’s shrine has one (Judg 17:5, 18:14–20). The legitimate Aaronide ephod is precisely calibrated; the unauthorized lay ephods that proliferate are precisely the cultic decay the deuteronomistic editor critiques. The verse is the institutional foundation for one of the OT’s clearest cases of a single object whose legitimate and illegitimate uses run through the entire historical narrative.

↩ ◇ Note. The golden calf. Bull-imagery for high gods was widespread in the ANE — El at Ugarit was titled "Bull El," and bull-iconography accompanied Hadad/Baal across Canaan and Egypt’s Apis. Aaron’s declaration "These are your gods, Israel, which brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (32:4) and his proclamation of "a feast to Yahweh" the next day (32:5) suggest the calf was meant as a Yahwistic image, not an alternative deity — a violation of the second commandment (image of Yahweh) rather than the first (other gods). The episode’s structural placement is devastating: the people violate the first principle of the just-given covenant while Moses is still on the mountain receiving the rest of it. Jeroboam’s later golden calves at Bethel and Dan (1 Kgs 12:28) deliberately echo this episode, with the same proclamation almost word-for-word — registering the deuteronomistic editor’s judgment that Jeroboam reproduces Aaron’s sin at the institutional founding of the northern kingdom. The chapter is the foundational anti-syncretist text in the entire OT.

↩ ◇ Note. "Face to face." The phrase panim el panim ("face to face") is the OT’s most intimate idiom for divine encounter, applied here to Moses and to no one else in the Pentateuch except in retrospective summaries (Deut 34:10, "no prophet has arisen since in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face"). The phrase stands in productive tension with 33:20 ("you cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live") just verses later — the same chapter that asserts "face to face" intimacy denies that any human can survive seeing Yahweh’s face. Most readers (so Childs, Brueggemann) take the apparent contradiction as deliberate: "face to face" describes the unmediated quality of communication, not literal visual experience. Paul’s eschatological hope at 1 Cor 13:12 ("now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face") draws on this Mosaic framework — direct, unmediated knowledge as the eschatological promise. The verse is the OT’s definitive prophetic-paradigm formulation, against which all other prophetic experience is measured.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EMBROIDER The art of embroidery was known to the Jews (Exodus 26:36; 35:35; 38:23; Judges 5:30; Psalm 45:14). The skill of the women in this art was seen in the preparation of the sacerdotal robes of the high priest (Exodus 28). It seems that the art became hereditary in certain families (1 Chronicles 4:21). The Assyrians were also noted for their embroidered robes (Ezekiel 27:24).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). THUMMIM perfection (LXX., “truth;” Vulg., “veritas”), Exodus 28:30; Deuteronomy 33:8; Judges 1:1; 20:18; 1 Samuel 14:3,18; 23:9; 2 Samuel 21:1. What the “Urim and Thummim” were cannot be determined with any certainty. All we certainly know is that they were a certain divinely-given means by which God imparted, through the high priest, direction and counsel to Israel when these were needed. The method by which this was done can be only a matter of mere conjecture. They were apparently material objects, quite distinct from the breastplate, but something added to it after all the stones had been set in it, something in addition to the breastplate and its jewels. They may have been, as some suppose, two small images, like the teraphim (comp. Judges 17:5; 18:14, 17, 20; Hos. 3:4), which were kept in the bag of the breastplate, by which, in some unknown way, the high priest could give forth his divinely imparted decision when consulted. They were probably lost at the destruction of the temple by Nebuchadnezzar. They were never seen after the return from captivity.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HEAD-DRESS Not in common use among the Hebrews. It is first mentioned in Exodus 28:40 (A.V., “bonnets;” R.V., “head-tires”). It was used especially for purposes of ornament (Job 29:14; Isaiah 3:23; 62:3). The Hebrew word here used, tsaniph, properly means a turban, folds of linen wound round the head. The Hebrew word peer, used in Isaiah 61:3, there rendered “beauty” (A.V.) and “garland” (R.V.), is a head-dress or turban worn by females (Isaiah 3: 20, “bonnets”), priests (Exodus 39:28), a bridegroom (Isaiah 61:10, “ornament;” R.V., “garland”). Ezekiel 16:10 and Jonah 2:5 are to be understood of the turban wrapped round the head. The Hebrew shebisim (Isaiah 3:18), in the Authorized Version rendered “cauls,” and marg. “networks,” denotes probably a kind of netted head-dress. The “horn” (Hebrews keren) mentioned in 1 Samuel 2:1 is the head-dress called by the Druses of Mount Lebanon the tantura.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MESSIAH (Hebrews mashiah), in all the thirty-nine instances of its occurring in the Old Testament, is rendered by the LXX. “Christos.” It means anointed. Thus priests (Exodus 28:41; 40:15; Numbers 3:3), prophets (1 Kings 19:16), and kings (1 Samuel 9:16; 16:3; 2 Samuel 12:7) were anointed with oil, and so consecrated to their respective offices. The great Messiah is anointed “above his fellows” (Psalm 45:7); i.e., he embraces in himself all the three offices. The Greek form “Messias” is only twice used in the New Testament, in John 1:41 and 4:25 (R.V., “Messiah”), and in the Old Testament the word Messiah, as the rendering of the Hebrew, occurs only twice (Dan 9:25, 26; R.V., “the anointed one”). The first great promise (Genesis 3:15) contains in it the germ of all the prophecies recorded in the Old Testament regarding the coming of the Messiah and the great work he was to accomplish on earth. The prophecies became more definite and fuller as the ages rolled on; the light shone more and more unto the perfect day. Different periods of prophetic revelation have been pointed out, (1) the patriarchal; (2) the Mosaic; (3) the period of David; (4) the period of prophetism, i.e., of those prophets whose works form a part of the Old Testament canon. The expectations of the Jews were thus kept alive from generation to generation, till the “fulness of the times,” when Messiah came, “made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law.” In him all these ancient prophecies have their fulfilment. Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah, the great Deliverer who was to come. (Comp. Matthew 26:54; Mark 9:12; Luke 18:31; 22:37; John 5:39; Acts 2; 16:31; 26:22, 23.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GALBANUM Hebrews helbenah, (Exodus 30:34), one of the ingredients in the holy incense. It is a gum, probably from the Galbanum officinale.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). INCENSE a fragrant composition prepared by the “art of the apothecary.” It consisted of four ingredients “beaten small” (Exodus 30:34-36). That which was not thus prepared was called “strange incense” (30:9). It was offered along with every meat-offering; and besides was daily offered on the golden altar in the holy place, and on the great day of atonement was burnt by the high priest in the holy of holies (30:7, 8). It was the symbol of prayer (Psalm 141:1,2; Revelation 5:8; 8:3, 4).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ONYCHA a nail; claw; hoof, (Hebrews sheheleth; Exodus 30:34), a Latin word applied to the operculum, i.e., the claw or nail of the strombus or wing-shell, a univalve common in the Red Sea. The opercula of these shell-fish when burned emit a strong odour “like castoreum.” This was an ingredient in the sacred incense.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). STACTE (Hebrews nataph), one of the components of the perfume which was offered on the golden altar (Exodus 30:34; R.V. marg., “opobalsamum”). The Hebrew word is from a root meaning “to distil,” and it has been by some interpreted as distilled myrrh. Others regard it as the gum of the storax tree, or rather shrub, the Styrax officinale. “The Syrians value this gum highly, and use it medicinally as an emulcent in pectoral complaints, and also in perfumery.”

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (363). Ephrem the Syrian Sermo de Domino Nostro (c. 363 AD)

'There shall no man see me and live' — and yet Moses sees the Lord's back as he passes by. Ephrem reads the verse as the canonical disclosure that full vision of God is reserved for the Incarnation: only when the Word is made flesh may humanity behold the divine face without being consumed. Tewahedo reads Ex 33:20 and 1 Jn 1:1 ('which we have seen with our eyes') as a single canonical arc from veiled vision to face-to-face Word.

↩ ◇ Athanasius of Alexandria (350). Athanasius of Alexandria Orationes contra Arianos III.14 (c. 350 AD)

'And he said, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live' — Athanasius marks ou dynēsē idein mou to prosōpon (thou canst not see my face) as the UNSEEABLE-FATHER / VISIBLE-WORD distinction. The Father-in-his-essence is unseeable (1 Tim 6:16 oude idein tis dynatai); what Moses is granted to see (LXX ta opisthia — 'the back parts') is the visible-condescension of the Word-pre-incarnate. Athanasius reads the Word as the agent of EVERY OT theophany (the burning bush, the pillar of cloud, the man-Yahweh at Mamre, the Sinai-glory) — the Father is never seen, only the Word who is the Father's-form-and-image. This hermeneutic grounds the Tewahedo iconographic-convention: the Father is never directly-depicted, only the Word-incarnate.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). COMMANDMENTS , THE TEN (Exodus 34:28; Deuteronomy 10:4, marg. “ten words”) i.e., the Decalogue (q.v.), is a summary of the immutable moral law. These commandments were first given in their written form to the people of Israel when they were encamped at Sinai, about fifty days after they came out of Egypt (Exodus 19:10-25). They were written by the finger of God on two tables of stone. The first tables were broken by Moses when he brought them down from the mount (32:19), being thrown by him on the ground. At the command of God he took up into the mount two other tables, and God wrote on them “the words that were on the first tables” (34:1). These tables were afterwards placed in the ark of the covenant (Deuteronomy 10:5; 1 Kings 8:9). Their subsequent history is unknown. They are as a whole called “the covenant” (Deuteronomy 4:13), and “the tables of the covenant” (9:9, 11; Hebrews 9:4), and “the testimony.” They are obviously “ten” in number, but their division is not fixed, hence different methods of numbering them have been adopted. The Jews make the “Preface” one of the commandments, and then combine the first and second. The Roman Catholics and Lutherans combine the first and second and divide the tenth into two. The Jews and Josephus divide them equally. The Lutherans and Roman Catholics refer three commandments to the first table and seven to the second. The Greek and Reformed Churches refer four to the first and six to the second table. The Samaritans add to the second that Gerizim is the mount of worship. (See LAW.)

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Moses descends with face shining and must put on a veil that the people may bear his presence. Paul reads the veil as the figure of the obscurity that remains over the OT until Christ takes it away (2 Cor 3:13-16). Ephrem follows Paul and reads Ex 34:30 as the canonical anchor of the veiled-to-unveiled progression: in the OT the prophet's borrowed glory must be covered; in the NT the believer beholds the Lord's own glory unveiled.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ENGRAVER Hebrews harash (Exodus 35:35; 38:23) means properly an artificer in wood, stone, or metal. The chief business of the engraver was cutting names or devices on rings and seals and signets (Exodus 28:11, 21, 36; Genesis 38:18).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WEAVING , WEAVERS Weaving was an art practised in very early times (Exodus 35:35). The Egyptians were specially skilled in it (Isaiah 19:9; Ezekiel 27:7), and some have regarded them as its inventors. In the wilderness, the Hebrews practised it (Exodus 26:1, 8; 28:4, 39; Leviticus 13:47). It is referred to in subsequent times as specially the women’s work (2 Kings 23:7; Proverbs 31:13, 24). No mention of the loom is found in Scripture, but we read of the “shuttle” (Job 7:6), “the pin” of the beam (Judges 16:14), “the web” (13, 14), and “the beam” (1 Samuel 17:7; 2 Samuel 21:19). The rendering, “with pining sickness,” in Isaiah 38:12 (A.V.) should be, as in the Revised Version, “from the loom,” or, as in the margin, “from the thrum.” We read also of the “warp” and “woof” (Leviticus 13:48, 49, 51-53, 58, 59), but the Revised Version margin has, instead of “warp,” “woven or knitted stuff.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEKAH Both the name and its explanation, “a half shekel,” are given in Exodus 38:26. The word properly means a “division,” a “part.” (R.V., “beka.”)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CENSUS There are five instances of a census of the Jewish people having been taken. (1.) In the fourth month after the Exodus, when the people were encamped at Sinai. The number of men from twenty years old and upward was then 603,550 (Exodus 38:26). (2.) Another census was made just before the entrance into Canaan, when the number was found to be 601,730, showing thus a small decrease (Numbers 26:51). (3.) The next census was in the time of David, when the number, exclusive of the tribes of Levi and Benjamin, was found to be 1,300,000 (2 Samuel 24:9; 1 Chronicles 21:5). (4.) Solomon made a census of the foreigners in the land, and found 153,600 able-bodied workmen (2 Chronicles 2:17, 18). (5.) After the return from Exile the whole congregation of Israel was numbered, and found to amount to 42,360 (Ezra 2:64). A census was made by the Roman government in the time of our Lord (Luke 2:1). (See TAXING.)

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:1.

Moreover thou shalt make the tabernacle [with] ten curtains [of] fine twined linen, and blue, and purple, and scarlet: [with] cherubims of cunning work shalt thou make them.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְאֶת־הַמִּשְׁכָּ֥ן תַּעֲשֶׂ֖ה עֶ֣שֶׂר יְרִיעֹ֑ת שֵׁ֣שׁ מָשְׁזָ֗ר וּתְכֵ֤לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָן֙ וְתֹלַ֣עַת שָׁנִ֔י כְּרֻבִ֛ים מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה חֹשֵׁ֖ב תַּעֲשֶׂ֥ה אֹתָֽם׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Καὶ τὴν σκηνὴν ποιήσεις δέκα αὐλαίας ἐκ βύσσου κεκλωσμένης καὶ ὑακίνθου καὶ πορφύρας καὶ κοκκίνου κεκλωσμένου· χερουβεὶμ ἐργασίᾳ ὑφάντου ποιήσεις αὐτάς.

Douay-Rheims

And thou shalt make the tabernacle in this manner: Thou shalt make ten curtains of fine twisted linen, and violet and purple, and scarlet twice dyed, diversified with embroidery.

JPS (1917)

Moreover thou shalt make the tabernacle with ten curtains: of fine twined linen, and blue, and purple, and scarlet, with cherubim the work of the skilful workman shalt thou make them.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Tabernaculum vero ita facies: decem cortinas de bysso retorta, et hyacintho, ac purpura, coccoque bis tincto, variatas opere plumario facies.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

«وَأَمَّا ٱلْمَسْكَنُ فَتَصْنَعُهُ مِنْ عَشَرِ شُقَقِ بُوصٍ مَبْرُومٍ وَأَسْمَانْجُونِيٍّ وَأُرْجُوَانٍ وَقِرْمِزٍ. بِكَرُوبِيمَ صَنْعَةَ حَائِكٍ حَاذِقٍ تَصْنَعُهَا.

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:2.

The length of one curtain [shall be] eight and twenty cubits, and the breadth of one curtain four cubits: and every one of the curtains shall have one measure.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

אֹ֣רֶךְ ׀ הַיְרִיעָ֣ה הָֽאַחַ֗ת שְׁמֹנֶ֤ה וְעֶשְׂרִים֙ בָּֽאַמָּ֔ה וְרֹ֨חַב֙ אַרְבַּ֣ע בָּאַמָּ֔ה הַיְרִיעָ֖ה הָאֶחָ֑ת מִדָּ֥ה אַחַ֖ת לְכָל־הַיְרִיעֹֽת׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

μῆκος τῆς αὐλαίας τῆς μιᾶς ὀκτὼ καὶ εἴκοσι πήχεων, καὶ εὖρος τεσσάρων πήχεων ἡ αὐλαία ἡ μία ἔσται· μέτρον τὸ αὐτὸ ἔσται πάσαις ταῖς αὐλαίαις.

Douay-Rheims

The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, the breadth shall be four cubits. All the curtains shall be of one measure.

JPS (1917)

The length of each curtain shall be eight and twenty cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits; all the curtains shall have one measure.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Longitudo cortinæ unius habebit viginti octo cubitos: latitudo, quatuor cubitorum erit. Unius mensuræ fient universa tentoria.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

طُولُ ٱلشُّقَّةِ ٱلْوَاحِدَةِ ثَمَانٍ وَعِشْرُونَ ذِرَاعًا، وَعَرْضُ ٱلشُّقَّةِ ٱلْوَاحِدَةِ أَرْبَعُ أَذْرُعٍ. قِيَاسًا وَاحِدًا لِجَمِيعِ ٱلشُّقَقِ.

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:3.

The five curtains shall be coupled together one to another; and [other] five curtains [shall be] coupled one to another.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

חֲמֵ֣שׁ הַיְרִיעֹ֗ת תִּֽהְיֶ֨יןָ֙ חֹֽבְרֹ֔ת אִשָּׁ֖ה אֶל־אֲחֹתָ֑הּ וְחָמֵ֤שׁ יְרִיעֹת֙ חֹֽבְרֹ֔ת אִשָּׁ֖ה אֶל־אֲחֹתָֽהּ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

πέντε δὲ αὐλαῖαι ἔσονται ἐξ ἀλλήλων ἐχόμεναι ἡ ἑτέρα ἐκ τῆς ἑτέρας, καὶ πέντε αὐλαῖαι ἔσονται συνεχόμεναι ἑτέρα τῇ ἑτέρᾳ.

Douay-Rheims

JPS (1917)

Five curtains shall be coupled together one to another; and the other five curtains shall be coupled one to another.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Quinque cortinæ sibi jungentur mutuo, et aliæ quinque nexu simili cohærebunt.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

تَكُونُ خَمْسٌ مِنَ ٱلشُّقَقِ بَعْضُهَا مَوْصُولٌ بِبَعْضٍ، وَخَمْسُ شُقَقٍ بَعْضُهَا مَوْصُولٌ بِبَعْضٍ.

↩

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:4.

And thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling; and likewise shalt thou make in the uttermost edge of [another] curtain, in the coupling of the second.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

וְעָשִׂ֜יתָ לֻֽלְאֹ֣ת תְּכֵ֗לֶת עַ֣ל שְׂפַ֤ת הַיְרִיעָה֙ הָאֶחָ֔ת מִקָּצָ֖ה בַּחֹבָ֑רֶת וְכֵ֤ן תַּעֲשֶׂה֙ בִּשְׂפַ֣ת הַיְרִיעָ֔ה הַקִּ֣יצוֹנָ֔ה בַּמַּחְבֶּ֖רֶת הַשֵּׁנִֽית׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ ποιήσεις αὐταῖς ἀγκύλας ὑακινθίνας ἐπὶ τοῦ χείλους τῆς αὐλαίας τῆς μιᾶς ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς μέρους τὴν συμβολήν· καὶ οὕτως ποιήσεις ἐπὶ τοῦ χείλους τῆς αὐλαίας τῆς ἐξωτέρας πρὸς τῇ συμβολῇ τῇ δευτέρᾳ.

Douay-Rheims

Thou shalt make loops of violet in the sides and tops of the curtains, that they may be joined one to another.

JPS (1917)

And thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain that is outmost in the first set; and likewise shalt thou make in the edge of the curtain that is outmost in the second set.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Ansulas hyacinthinas in lateribus ac summitatibus facies cortinarum, ut possint invicem copulari.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

وَتَصْنَعُ عُرًى مِنْ أَسْمَانْجُونِيٍّ عَلَى حَاشِيَةِ ٱلشُّقَّةِ ٱلْوَاحِدَةِ فِي ٱلطَّرَفِ مِنَ ٱلْمُوَصَّلِ ٱلْوَاحِدِ. وَكَذَلِكَ تَصْنَعُ فِي حَاشِيَةِ ٱلشُّقَّةِ ٱلطَّرَفِيَّةِ مِنَ ٱلْمُوَصَّلِ ٱلثَّانِي.

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:5.

Fifty loops shalt thou make in the one curtain, and fifty loops shalt thou make in the edge of the curtain that [is] in the coupling of the second; that the loops may take hold one of another.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

חֲמִשִּׁ֣ים לֻֽלָאֹ֗ת תַּעֲשֶׂה֮ בַּיְרִיעָ֣ה הָאֶחָת֒ וַחֲמִשִּׁ֣ים לֻֽלָאֹ֗ת תַּעֲשֶׂה֙ בִּקְצֵ֣ה הַיְרִיעָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֖ר בַּמַּחְבֶּ֣רֶת הַשֵּׁנִ֑ית מַקְבִּילֹת֙ הַלֻּ֣לָאֹ֔ת אִשָּׁ֖ה אֶל־אֲחֹתָֽהּ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

πεντήκοντα ἀγκύλας ποιήσεις τῇ αὐλαίᾳ τῇ μιᾷ, καὶ πεντήκοντα ἀγκύλας ποιήσεις ἐκ τοῦ μέρους τῆς αὐλαίας κατὰ τὴν συμβολὴν τῆς δευτέρας· ἀντιπρόσωποι ἀντιπίπτουσαι ἀλλήλαις εἰς ἑκάστην.

Douay-Rheims

Every curtain shall have fifty loops on both sides, so set on, that one loop may be against another loop, and one may be fitted to the other.

JPS (1917)

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Arabic (Van Dyck)

خَمْسِينَ عُرْوَةً تَصْنَعُ فِي ٱلشُّقَّةِ ٱلْوَاحِدَةِ، وَخَمْسِينَ عُرْوَةً تَصْنَعُ فِي طَرَفِ ٱلشُّقَّةِ ٱلَّذِي فِي ٱلْمُوَصَّلِ ٱلثَّانِي. تَكُونُ ٱلْعُرَى بَعْضُهَا مُقَابِلٌ لِبَعْضٍ.

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:6.

And thou shalt make fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

Douay-Rheims

JPS (1917)

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Arabic (Van Dyck)

The Second Book of Moses, Exodus 26:7.

¶ And thou shalt make curtains [of] goats’ [hair] to be a covering upon the tabernacle: eleven curtains shalt thou make.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

JPS (1917)

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Douay-Rheims
